source_text: Nam illa altera reliquorum dementia est manifesta otiosis hominibns negotiatio: in iniuriam suam pinguescit in sagina corpus ut robustius aut feriat aut uapulet, et prima uictoria est ultra modum, humani uentris esurire potuisse, super titulo coronae edacis flagitiosae nundinae: ictibus infelix facies locatur, ut infelicior uenter saginetur. quam foeda praeterea ipsa luctamina, uir infra uirum iacens am* plexibus inhonestis et nexibus implicatur. in tali certamine stare. uiderit quis uincat, pudor uictus est. ecce tibi alter nudus salit, alter orbem aeneum contentis in aerem uiribus iactat. haec gloria eat dementiae. denique remoue spectatorem, reddideris uanitatem. fugienda sunt ista christianis fidelibus, ut iam frequenter diximus, tam uana, tam perniciosa, tam sacrilega spectacula: et oculi nostri sunt et aures custodiendae. cito in hoc assuescimus quod audimus, celere in id quod uidemus. nam cum mens hominis ad uitia ipsa ducitur, sibi quid faciet, si habuerit exempla? natura corporis lubrica quae sponte corruit quid faciet, si fuerit impulsa ? auocandus est animus ab istis.
thought_title: The madness of athletic contests and the need to guard eyes and ears
orientation: Novatian continues his catalogue of public shows, now turning from stage plays to the athletic contests and their bodily harm and shamelessness.
pass_a_gloss: For that other madness of the remaining men is a manifest business for idle men: the body grows fat in its own injury with stuffing so that it may strike or be beaten more strongly, and the first victory is to have been able to be hungry beyond measure of the human belly, upon the title of a crown of a gluttonous shameful market: the unhappy face is hired out for blows, so that the more unhappy belly may be stuffed. How foul besides are the wrestlings themselves, a man lying under a man is entangled with dishonorable embraces and bindings. To stand in such a contest. Let him see who wins, modesty has been defeated. Behold for you another man leaps naked, another throws a bronze hoop into the air with strained strength. Let this glory be of madness. Finally remove the spectator, you will have returned vanity. These things must be fled by faithful Christians, as we have now said frequently, such vain, such pernicious, such sacrilegious public shows: both our eyes and our ears must be guarded. We quickly grow accustomed to this which we hear, quickly to that which we see. For when the mind of a man is led to vices themselves, what will it do for itself, if it has had examples? The slippery nature of the body which falls of its own accord, what will it do, if it has been pushed? The soul must be called away from these things.

choices.why: Keeps the commercial metaphor of the passage, where bodies are hired out and fed for profit in the contests.
Conveys the crude force-feeding image of athletes fattening themselves, matching the passage's disgust.
Preserves the image of the contest as a shameful marketplace where faces are hired and bellies stuffed.
Plural rendering keeps the concrete, repeated nature of the bouts Novatian condemns.
Keeps the passive perfect force and the personification of modesty as the real loser.
Renders the gerundive of obligation, matching Novatian's moral command to the faithful.

pass_b_english: The other madness of the rest is plain to see: it is a business for idle men. A body grows fat on stuffing to its own injury, so that it may strike harder or be beaten harder, and the first victory is to have been able to hunger beyond the measure of a human belly—all for the title of a crown in a shameful market of gluttons. An unhappy face is hired out for blows, so that a still more unhappy belly may be stuffed. How foul, moreover, are the wrestlings themselves: a man lies under a man, tangled in dishonorable embraces and bindings. In such a contest, let whoever wins be seen—modesty has been defeated. Look, one man leaps naked; another hurls a bronze hoop into the air with all his strength. This is the glory of madness. Take away the spectator, and you have returned it to vanity. Faithful Christians must flee these things, as we have said often already—public shows so vain, so pernicious, so sacrilegious. Both our eyes and our ears must be guarded. We quickly grow accustomed to what we hear, and swiftly to what we see. For when the human mind is led to vices themselves, what will it do to itself if it has examples? The body's nature is slippery and falls of its own accord—what will it do if it is pushed? The soul must be called away from these things.
notes: The source text contains 'am* plexibus' with an asterisk, indicating possible OCR damage or a line break in the manuscript; the gloss treats it as 'amplexibus' (embraces).
